opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people assume you need a PhD in machine learning to work here, and that's really not the case. Honestly, a lot of the most impactful people on the teams I've worked with came from strong software engineering backgrounds rather than research. So much of what makes large-scale model training work is engineering: building reliable infrastructure, debugging distributed systems, making things run efficiently on huge clusters, writing code that other people can actually build on. Those skills are scarce, and they transfer really well.

On the research side, what I look for is less about credentials and more about whether someone can take an ambiguous question, design a clean experiment, and actually get a trustworthy answer. A lot of ML research is noisy, and the people who do well are careful. They check their baselines, they're skeptical of results that look too good, and they move quickly without cutting corners on correctness.

And I'd say the other piece is genuinely caring about the mission. We're working on systems that could be really transformative, and we want people who take safety seriously and think about the consequences of what they're building, not just people excited about scaling things up. That doesn't mean everyone needs to be an alignment expert on day one. But you should be someone who's willing to engage with those questions and change your mind when the evidence points somewhere new.

So if someone is listening and thinking, "I'm a good engineer but I don't have an ML background," I'd encourage them to just start. Read the papers, reimplement some things, train small models, and get your hands dirty. You can get surprisingly far in a few months, and that practical experience counts for a lot more than people expect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a lot less prescriptive than people assume. People often come to me thinking there's some specific credential they need — a PhD in machine learning, publications at NeurIPS, that kind of thing. And for some roles, especially on the research side, that background is genuinely useful. But it's not the thing we're actually selecting for.

What we're really looking for is something closer to: can you take a hard, poorly-specified problem and make progress on it? A lot of the work on the pretraining team, for instance, is engineering. It's distributed systems, it's debugging why a training run slowed down by 10 percent, it's figuring out why some metric looks weird. You need to be comfortable with a lot of uncertainty and with the fact that nobody can tell you the right answer, because nobody knows it.

My own path is a decent illustration. I didn't come in with a traditional ML research background. I did a lot of software engineering, I worked on applied ML problems, and I learned the research side mostly by doing it alongside people who were better at it than I was. I think that's actually pretty common here. Some of the strongest people I work with came from backgrounds like physics, or from being very good general-purpose software engineers who picked up the ML.

So if someone asked me what to do, I'd say: get really good at engineering. Write a lot of code. Build things end to end. Implement a few ML papers from scratch so you understand what's going on under the hood, and then try to go a step beyond what the paper did. That process of hitting a wall, not knowing why, and figuring it out — that's most of the job. If you can demonstrate that, the specific credentials matter a lot less than people think.

r001.rationale: It says a PhD is useful for some research roles but is not what Anthropic is selecting for, and that specific credentials matter much less.

r002.rationale: It recommends practicing work that mirrors the job: writing code, building things end to end, implementing ML papers, and troubleshooting problems.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on the role. There isn’t one background that’s right for working at Anthropic. For some research roles, experience in machine learning is very useful. But there’s also a lot of work where the central skill is being a really strong software engineer: being able to understand a complicated system, figure out why something isn’t working, and make it better.

I wouldn’t treat having a PhD, or having worked on AI before, as a universal prerequisite. What matters is what you can do, how quickly you can learn, and whether you can work well with other people on problems where the answer isn’t already clear.

And I think it’s valuable to be interested in the broader purpose of the work. You don’t need to arrive with a settled view on every question about AI safety, but you should be willing to take those questions seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says a PhD is not a universal prerequisite for working at Anthropic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on the role. For some research roles, having a strong machine learning background is very helpful. But I wouldn’t want people to conclude that you need a PhD, or that you need to have spent years working specifically on AI safety.

There’s a lot of work that requires really good engineering: building reliable systems, running experiments, understanding why something isn’t working. Someone who’s an excellent software engineer can bring a lot to that work, even if they have quite a bit of machine learning to learn.

The broader things I’d look for are whether you can learn quickly, whether you exercise good judgment, and whether you can work well with other people on problems where nobody knows the answer yet. And I’d encourage people to look at the particular role rather than trying to decide whether they have the right background for Anthropic in general.
